title: Written letters and sound symbols
summary: The book gives seven written vowels a e ɛ i o ɔ u. Its notes say c and h occur together as ch, and n and y can form ny. ŋ can begin a word. Phonetic vowel symbols describe pronunciation rather than extra ordinary written letters. The consonant list contains apparent transcription/count errors; consult the orthography guide for keyboard spelling.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Vowel harmony and endings
summary: Vowel sounds fall into open and close sets. An ending must agree with the stem's vowel set: the book contrasts pa plus e giving pae, and su plus i giving sui.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Long vowels and consonants
summary: A double vowel marks vowel length. Some noun and adjective plurals have long consonants, especially in class D. Preserve these distinctions when looking up forms.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Tone distinctions in this grammar
summary: Tone is part of a word's pronunciation. This grammar describes low mid high and rising tones but usually leaves tone unwritten. It explicitly marks á plural you, ná if, bá will not and wó will to distinguish them from other words. This is a source-specific convention, not a general accent rule.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Pronunciation and written forms
summary: The notes discuss r between vowels, d at the beginning of simple words, and d inside words with distinct parts. They also explain that ei can represent different vowel sounds according to word position. Phonetic examples remain pronunciation evidence rather than keyboard suggestions.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Greetings and responses
summary: Greetings depend on time of day, the number of listeners, situation, locality and preference. Exchanges can continue through several questions and responses. naa can accompany greetings wishes and exhortations. Use the printed dialogues as source examples, not universal responses.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Pronouncing the written pronoun n
summary: The written singular you pronoun n is commonly pronounced m before p b or m, and n before k g or n. Its realization before w can vary. The spelling remains n in the book's examples.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Questions for learning Kasem
summary: The book supplies questions about names origin meanings and what things are called or used for, along with requests to repeat and speak carefully. These are recorded complete expressions, not templates for generating new translations.
examples: Ba bwoi konto we bɛ mo?
N ma konto n ke bɛ mo?
What do you use that for?
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Subject verb and object order
summary: The ordinary order is subject then verb then object. A clause can have no object. A small group of verbs including bere show, pa give and ke do or make can take two objects.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Adverbs time and place in clauses
summary: Adverb time and place expressions normally follow the subject verb and object. When an adverb occurs with time or place material, the adverb comes first. The book says multiple adverb time and place phrases in one clause are unusual.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Descriptive clauses and strong forms
summary: Descriptive verbs say what the subject is like. Some descriptive forms with n have a strong form with mm instead. The editable list has transcription damage, so use its clearly printed examples without inventing replacement forms.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Equative clauses with ye and dae
summary: An equative clause relates a subject to a noun or adjective complement using ye. Its negative counterpart uses dae. This differs from describing a subject's location.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Location with wo tere wora and tera
summary: A location clause uses wo and a place expression; its negative is tere. wora combines wo and da and means be there; tera is its negative. Depending on context, being there can also refer to being around or still alive.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Clauses without a verb
summary: Some clauses have a subject and complement without a verb. In the examples, mo follows the subject. These are a stated exception to the usual verb-containing clause patterns.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Fronting and emphasis with mo
summary: An element can move to the beginning of a clause and be followed by mo, drawing attention to that element. This often answers a question. Question elements usually come first with mo. Some short time words can also occur between subject and verb.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Weak personal pronouns
summary: Personal pronouns have subject and object forms. Singular subject forms are a n o; corresponding object forms are ne m o. Plural forms include dé debam, á abam and ba ba. Short object pronouns can be closely joined to a verb with a hyphen, and their tones differ from subject forms.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Pronouns agree with noun class
summary: Impersonal pronouns vary by noun class and number. The tables retain each class's forms. The editable weak-pronoun table prints dé for class B singular while the noun-class table prints de; this discrepancy is preserved instead of silently resolved.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Strong pronouns
summary: Strong or emphatic pronouns have the same form for subject and object and do not change tone in that use. Personal forms include amo nmo omo or wonto, debam abam and bamo or banto. Modifiers can follow pronouns.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Articles and other noun modifiers
summary: The article follows the noun and agrees with its class and number. Demonstrative other some and certain forms also vary by class. The chart presents their order after the noun; not every modifier can occur together. This and other can sometimes precede the noun.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Numerals and modifiers in noun phrases
summary: Numerals two through seven and larger numerals containing them vary with noun class. One is dedoa and can agree with the noun. Numerals combine with demonstratives articles and modifiers such as all many only and also.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Relative clauses inside noun phrases
summary: Relative clauses contain na and usually end in to. They may be linked to a noun by a class-agreeing who or which form such as wolo balo delo or yalo. The book also records relatives without that linker or final to.
examples: swoona yalo o na di to
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Joining noun phrases with de
summary: de joins nouns or noun phrases with the meaning and. dedaane is a longer form. Clause joining uses a different construction described in chapter six.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Possession by phrase order
summary: A possessing noun phrase or pronoun comes before the possessed noun phrase. Several noun phrases can be linked, but only the first can be a pronoun. The source illustrates nested possession.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Adjectives and noun agreement
summary: Adjectives follow the noun. An accompanying article agrees with the adjective's class. Many nouns use shortened forms before an adjective; the adjective changes for number. Some adjectives can stand alone, and a few require na in that position.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Place time and ne phrases
summary: Place and time expressions can be single words, pairs of time words, noun phrases or phrases ending in ne. A position word can precede ne, including top back bottom mouth or side forms recorded in the source.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Adverb phrases
summary: Adverbs can be a single word or a longer expression. The book records well much twice often and happily, among others. Some time and adverb phrases at the beginning of a sentence can end in to.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Verb phrases contain verbs and particles
summary: A verb phrase can include a verb and words before it that express tense or other meanings. Chapter eight explains the particles and verb classes in detail.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Clause chains
summary: A clause chain repeats the first clause's subject as a weak pronoun in subsequent clauses. The first verb can show tense; following verbs usually stand without those tense words. Initial verbs can express adverbial meanings aspect ability or completion. Some adverbial constructions are exceptions.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Tone in repeated chain subjects
summary: Low-tone weak pronouns change to mid tone when repeated as subjects in ordinary clause chains; high-tone weak pronouns remain high. Chains expressing continuous action with wora are stated exceptions: their weak pronouns do not change tone.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Joining clauses with ye
summary: ye joins clauses or clause chains. An English and does not always correspond to ye: a Kasem clause chain can express the sequence without it.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Conditional and when clauses
summary: Conditional na follows the subject; the grammar distinguishes its tone from the na in past when clauses, which usually end in to. Conditional na can also refer to a when event that has not happened yet. The relevant verb uses a past form. These subordinate clauses precede the main clause.
examples: Debam na jwoori dé yi sɔŋɔ to
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Purpose clauses with se
summary: A purpose clause starts with se and follows the main clause. It can itself be a chain. Low-tone weak subjects following se change to mid tone in the described construction.
examples: A vei sɔŋɔ, se a saŋe wodiu a di
I went home to cook some food to eat
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Result clauses with pa or pa se
summary: A result clause begins with pa or pa se and follows the main clause. It can be a clause chain. The source examples distinguish this from purpose clauses.
examples: Ba mage debam, pa se dé duri dé vo sɔŋɔ
They beat us, and so we ran home
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Combining sentence parts
summary: A sentence can place conditional or when material before the main clause and purpose or result material after it. Conditional clauses can be joined with ye; purpose clauses can follow one another without ye.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Linking events with ma
summary: ma follows the first subject in the main clause and signals what happened next. It is common in narratives and uses consecutive single-action forms.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Five noun classes
summary: Nouns are grouped into classes A B C D E by their singular and plural pronouns and articles. Stems combine with suffixes; the book distinguishes consonant and vowel stems and describes class-specific changes. Class is not determined only by a noun's meaning.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Noun class A
summary: Class A uses o and ba, and articles wom and bam. Singular endings include o or u; plural endings include a and na. Many members denote people, but some people nouns belong to other classes.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Noun class B
summary: Class B uses de and ya, and dem and yam. Its typical singular suffix is e or i and plural suffix is a. Vowel-stem nouns have additional source-listed forms.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Noun class C
summary: Class C uses ka and se, and kam and sem. Its singular suffix is a. Plural formation depends on stem type; the source supplies r n l stems, g and ŋ stems, and vowel stems rather than one universal replacement.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Noun class D
summary: Class D uses ko and te, and kom and tem. Singular endings include u o ɔ; plural endings and stem changes can produce long vowels or consonants. The book notes dialect variation and exceptions, including g stems.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Noun class E
summary: Class E uses ko and de, and kom and dem. Singular endings include u o ɔ; plural endings include ne and ni, with other printed alternatives. Consult the paradigms for particular stems and dialect forms.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Mixed classes and plural-only nouns
summary: Some nouns combine a singular from one class with a plural from another. Some people nouns use class A agreement with class B endings. Some liquid nouns are recorded only in plural forms. The paradigms retain these exceptions.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Tense and kind of action
summary: The book distinguishes past present and future, and single completed versus continuous action. Verbs belong to classes A B C D according to how their forms change. Most verbs are described as class A; particles are shared across classes.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Past single action
summary: Classes A and D generally use e or i; vowel stems can occur without an added ending. Classes B and C use a in the past, with changes before objects or after the negative wo. The printed paradigms list the actual forms.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Future single action
summary: Future single action uses wó, or bá for its negative, with the source's ordinary unmarked variants also present. Classes A and D retain e or i forms; classes B and C use simpler forms, often losing a past g or n. The future form does not change before an object in this description.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Habitual continuous action
summary: Continuous action can describe repeated habits or action still in progress. Habitual class A and C forms commonly use a; class B and D forms use e or i. Some a endings change before an object. The negative particle is ba. Optional negative bundles in the source must not be quoted as one exact translation.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Present action in progress
summary: Many verbs use wora with a repeated subject and continuous-action form to describe action in progress. Other posture verbs can serve similarly. Motion verbs use maa instead; coming has different habitual and in-progress forms in the book.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Future continuous action
summary: Future particles combine with ta: wó ta for positive and bá ta for negative. Verb forms follow the continuous-action pattern, with relevant changes before an object. This section occurs twice in the editable source; the clearer duplicate supports the quoted examples.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Past continuous action
summary: Past continuous or habitual action uses the continuous forms with time words or particles such as ya or déem to locate the action in the past. The source also records an earlier ongoing interpretation.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Consecutive single action
summary: Consecutive forms express actions following one another. They use future single-action forms without future particles, including later links of clause chains and constructions after ma se pa or ye. Their endings do not change in the stated pattern.
examples: O vei o ga tɔnɔ o ti
He went and finished reading a book
O bá vo o ga tɔnɔ o ti
He will not go and finish reading a book
O ma vo o ga tɔnɔ
Then he went and read a book
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Commands and prohibitions
summary: Single-action and continuous commands differ. Continuous commands use ta and can include n or the plural pronoun. Negative commands use yé; plural commands often add na. Most single-action commands use the simple or future form, with class C exceptions and explicitly listed irregular forms.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Particle and verb-form summaries
summary: The verb table organizes continuous past future and command forms by class, showing different pre-object forms in parentheses. The particle summary in the editable copy is damaged and is not used to manufacture missing cells. Clear prose and the complete verb table remain available.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Small words before verbs
summary: The book distinguishes ma for the next single event and maa for additional facts or motion in progress. It also discusses laam daa nam ya deem and doom for sequence repetition contrast and time. Their tone and context matter; they are not interchangeable English words.
examples: And he was there for a long time
O laam ma zaje ovo sɔŋɔ
Then he got up and went home
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Commands attention and focus particles
summary: na can follow plural commands; naa holds attention in greetings and instructions; mo draws attention to new information. These uses differ from conditional and question uses of similar written forms.
examples: Dé vo se dé ba naa
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Yes or no questions
summary: na can occur at the end of a yes or no question, often after mo. It can be omitted with lengthening and falling intonation. Printed question punctuation does not replace the pronunciation evidence.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.

title: Asking for information
summary: The source lists where what who whose which when how many how and why expressions. Some question words or forms agree with noun class or number. Quote the complete printed questions; do not compose a new question from isolated entries.
attribution: P. L. Hewer, A Basic Grammar of Kasem, GILLBT. First printed 1983; supplied 2014 printing. Copyright GILLBT retained.
note: Source-backed paraphrase. Consult the chapter reference for the printed tables, examples and transcription limitations.
